rebuttal

rih-BUT-ul -- three syllables, stress on the second syllable, BUT. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Rebuttal is an attempt to refute an argument.

Each debater is given four minutes for a rebuttal before the judges score the round.

Example

A columnist writes that the new bike lanes have made traffic worse. The following week the city's traffic engineer publishes a piece of her own, walking through the count data street by street and showing that delays actually fell.

The engineer's piece is a rebuttal -- an attempt to refute the argument by answering it directly, with evidence. A rebuttal is more than disagreement: it takes the other side's claim apart.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

counterargument: A counterargument is any argument raised against another -- it may be offered calmly, in advance, even inside the same essay. A rebuttal is a directed answer: it takes a specific claim someone has made and pushes back at it, point by point, with reasons.

retort: A retort is a quick, sharp reply made on the spot -- wit, not evidence, is what makes it land. A rebuttal is slower, heavier machinery: a reasoned answer that takes an argument apart with reasons and proof.

denial: A denial simply says 'no, that is not true' and stops there. A rebuttal brings reasons: it answers the claim with evidence and argument. You can deny a charge in two words, but a rebuttal has to do the work of disproving it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

endorsement: a public statement of support

concession: an admission that the other side is right

Where it sits · how completely it knocks the argument down — objection → rebuttal → refutation

objection vs. rebuttal: An objection merely raises a doubt -- a hand goes up and a question is asked -- while a rebuttal answers the argument point by point and tries to knock it down.

refutation vs. rebuttal: Refutation is the strongest of the three: a rebuttal is the attempt, but a refutation is the success -- an argument actually proven wrong.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — re-

prefix — re-: back (Latin)

root — but-

root — but-: to strike, to thrust (Old French bo(u)ter)

suffix — -al

suffix — -al: the act of (Latin -alis)

Put it together

Put it together: Rebuttal joins re- ('back') with Old French buter, 'to strike or thrust' -- the same idea behind a goat butting with its head. A rebuttal strikes an argument straight back where it came from.

Use the root in a new word: buttress

Use the root in a new word: buttress: Stone buttresses thrust against the cathedral's walls to keep them from leaning outward.

Root Check

Word Choice

Rebuttal is the language of debate, law, and academic writing: offer a rebuttal, a point-by-point rebuttal, the rebuttal round. It always answers a specific argument, so it needs something to push back against. Simply saying 'no' is a denial; a rebuttal brings reasons.
